title: Robust Passive Quantum Memory in Three Dimensions, Part I: Thermal and Zero-Temperature Perturbative Stability
problem: A magnet stores a bit for years without any active correction, because a flip of the whole magnet must cross an energy barrier that grows with its size. Can a three-dimensional quantum system with local interactions do the same for a qubit? It would have to withstand two threats: heat, which creates defects at random, and small errors in the interactions themselves, which tilt the energy landscape. A construction by Balasubramanian, Davydova and Lin withstands heat in three dimensions, but whether it survives perturbations of the Hamiltonian was open, even at zero temperature.
result: A slight variant of that code family passes each test separately. Without perturbation it is a self-correcting memory below a positive critical temperature: coupled to a local Markovian thermal bath, the stored qubit survives for a time that grows as \(\exp(\Omega(N^\eta))\) with the number \(N\) of spins. At zero temperature, under any static perturbation of small enough local strength whose interactions decay faster than every power of the distance, the spectral gap stays at least \(\tfrac12\). The splitting of the two ground states then falls faster than any inverse power of \(N\), and suitably dressed logical operators protect the qubit for times longer than any power of \(N\). Standalone existence statements of the main conclusions are verified in Lean 4.
significance: Self-correction in three dimensions is one of the oldest open problems of topological quantum memory. Fracton codes reach only logarithmic barriers, and earlier welded codes lose their barrier to entropy at any positive temperature. This paper adds the missing zero-temperature stability. Its main technical point is general: local topological order may be weakened so that the neighbourhood needed to generate a stabilizer grows in proportion to its size, and the stability proof still works for perturbations that decay quickly enough. A companion, Part II, is announced for temperature and perturbation together.
limitations: The constants put the construction outside physics. Each step of the hierarchy scales lengths by \(5.4\times10^{24}\), the critical temperature is at most of order \(10^{-51}\) in units of the check energy, and the exponent is \(\eta\approx1.2\times10^{-3}\); the paper says so itself. Storing a state is shown, preparing one by cooling is not. The thermal theorem is for Markovian baths obeying detailed balance. The case with temperature and perturbation both nonzero is not proved here, and Part II was not found on arXiv when this entry was written. The paper states that the author set the direction, the problem and the overall strategy, that "Gemini 4 Argon performed most of the detailed mathematical reasoning and proof construction", and that Gemini 4 helped to draft the text. The Lean development certifies two existence theorems, not every lemma of the paper, and it omits the topological-order clause of the main theorem from its trusted statement. It was not re-run for this entry.

description: Kitaev's toric code in four dimensions is the model of a passive quantum memory. Errors are surfaces, their violated checks form loops, and loops cost energy in proportion to their length, so changing the stored state means crossing a barrier that grows with the system. In two dimensions violated checks are points that wander freely, and no such memory exists among local stabilizer codes. In three dimensions the toric code protects one kind of error and not the other, and translation-invariant stabilizer codes cannot have barriers above logarithmic size.

The code breaks translation invariance. It starts from a five-qubit planar surface code. Each odd step of a hierarchy replaces every \(X\)-check by a hollow cylinder of many qubits, with the cylinders welded where they meet. This keeps the stored qubit and amplifies the trail of violated checks that bit flips leave. Each even step does the same with \(X\) and \(Z\) exchanged. Between steps the picture is rescaled and its points are moved slightly, so that only a bounded number of qubits falls in any unit ball. The variant in this paper uses three layers in each cylinder instead of two, which turns ties into majorities.

The thermal argument reads syndromes from the top scale down. A local rule sweeps violated checks out of the cylinders and onto copies of the coarser checks. Because each coarse check is represented three times, the coarse syndrome has at most \(16/27\) of the weight after a full two-step cycle. A large error on the coarse level therefore needs a much larger set of violated checks below it, and at the top of \(k\) cycles the minimum weight is at least \((3/2)^k\). The decoder passes on only syndromes and one parity bit, not physical corrections. That avoids a discontinuity, which the paper exhibits, in which a single flipped qubit changes the physical correction by a large stabilizer.

The zero-temperature argument is a stability proof in the style of Bravyi, Hastings and Michalakis. Those proofs assume that a stabilizer supported in a ball of radius \(r\) is a product of checks in a ball of radius \(r+O(1)\). In a welded hierarchy this fails, because a loop that crosses a weld of size \(r\) is filled only by sweeping through cylinders of that size. The paper shows that a ball of radius \(Cr\) is enough, calls the property Relative Cone Acyclicity, and proves it by stopping the coarse-graining at the scale of the ball instead of continuing to the bottom.

Neither axis settles the interior, where heat and perturbation act together. The perturbation theory controls energies through an operator inequality, and the exponential function does not preserve operator inequalities, so thermal weights are not controlled in the same way. The abstract says that Part II fills this gap with a cluster expansion in imaginary time. For practice, the paper's first open problem is a construction with realistic parameters. It points to a deterministic version outlined by Balasubramanian, Davydova and Lin with a scale factor of 8, for which stability is not yet proved.

methods.explanation: A memory fails thermally when the syndrome contains a pattern that can mislead the decoder. The paper shows that every such pattern contains a small subset, a witness, from a pool that does not grow too fast, and that each witness has weight at least \((3/2)^k\). A Peierls argument then bounds the probability, with energy against the logarithm of the pool size.
math: For the pool, a coarse syndrome of weight \(w\) must come from a fine one of weight at least \(\tfrac{27}{16}w\), so the minimum weights obey \[w_0=1,\qquad w_{j+1}=\lceil27w_j/16\rceil,\] which gives \(1,2,4,7,12,\dots\), so \(w_{j+1}\ge\tfrac{27}{16}w_j>\tfrac32w_j\). Each step multiplies the number of witnesses by at most a constant to the power \(w_{j+1}\). The geometric sum of weights keeps the total at most \(B^{8w_k}\).

The probability that a thermal syndrome contains a given set \(\tau\) of violated checks is at most \(e^{-\beta|\tau|}\). Let \(\mathcal S\) be the linear space of realizable syndromes and \(g(u)=e^{-\beta|u|}\). If \(\sigma\supseteq\tau\), then \(|\sigma|=|\tau|+|\sigma\oplus\tau|\), so \[\sum_{\sigma\in\mathcal S,\,\sigma\supseteq\tau}e^{-\beta|\sigma|}\le e^{-\beta|\tau|}\sum_{u\in\tau\oplus\mathcal S}g(u).\] The Fourier coefficients of \(g\) are nonnegative. The sum of \(g\) over a coset of \(\mathcal S\) is \(|\mathcal S|\sum_{T\in\mathcal S^\perp}\hat g(T)(-1)^{T\cdot\tau}\), hence never larger than the sum over \(\mathcal S\) itself, which is the partition function.

The union bound over the pool gives \[\Pr[\text{unsafe}]\le B^{8w_k}e^{-\beta w_k}\le\tfrac12e^{-(\beta-\beta_c)w_k},\qquad\beta_c=8\ln B+O(1).\] Since the number of qubits is \(e^{O(k)}\), the weight \(w_k\ge(3/2)^k\) is a power \(N^\eta\), with \[\eta=\frac{\ln(3/2)}{6\ln\Lambda}\approx1.2\times10^{-3}\quad\text{for}\quad\Lambda=5.4\times10^{24}.\] The smallness of \(\eta\) and of the critical temperature both come from the enormous \(\Lambda\) and \(B\), not from the mechanism.
methods.transfer: The coset inequality holds for any linear set of syndromes, and replaces the usual argument of erasing a contour when defects cannot be removed one at a time. It is useful for thermal bounds on other stabilizer Hamiltonians, LDPC codes included, whenever one can exhibit a pool of witnesses whose size is exponential in their weight with a controlled base. It controls equilibrium probabilities; lifetimes need an additional argument about the dynamics.

methods.technique: Stability of the gap when the local neighbourhood grows linearly
methods.explanation: Relative Cone Acyclicity is a homological statement about filling loops. Linear duality turns it into the two operator conditions that a stability proof needs: local operators act as scalars on the ground space, and an operator that annihilates the ground space already annihilates the ground space of a ball \(C\) times larger. The dilation costs only polynomial factors, which a perturbation that decays faster than any power absorbs.
math: Let \(B\) be a ball of radius \(r\) and \(B^+\) the ball of radius \(\lceil Cr\rceil\). The condition says that every syndrome-free chain of qubits in \(B\) is a sum of checks inside \(B^+\), in both the \(X\) and the \(Z\) sector. Then a Pauli operator on \(B\) that commutes with all checks in \(B^+\) is a signed product of those checks. Expanding an arbitrary operator \(X\) on \(B\) in Pauli operators gives one scalar for both projectors, \[P_{B^+}XP_{B^+}=c(X)\,P_{B^+},\qquad P_0XP_0=c(X)\,P_0,\] with \(P_0\) the global and \(P_{B^+}\) the local ground-space projector. Applied to \(X=O^\dagger O\), it shows that \(OP_0=0\) implies \(OP_{B^+}=0\).

The same identity transfers norms. For \(S\) supported near a site, the operator \(M=P_{B'}SS^\dagger P_{B'}\), with \(B'\) the ball enlarged by one site, commutes with all checks. It therefore has the same scalar on \(P_0\) and on \(P_{B^+}\), and \[\|P_{B^+}S\|\le\|P_0S\|.\] After quasi-adiabatic continuation the perturbation is a sum of site terms that nearly annihilate the ground space. Cutting each at growing radii \(j\) and using the norm transfer writes it as a sum of terms \(D_j(u)\) that live strictly in the excited space of a ball of radius \(O(Cj)\), plus a negligible remainder.

A term that vanishes on the local ground space is controlled by the checks it can see, \[|\langle\psi,D_j(u)\psi\rangle|\le\|D_j(u)\|\sum_{i\,\subset\,C_j(u)}\langle\psi,Q_i\psi\rangle.\] Summing over sites, each check is counted at most \(O(C^3j^3)\) times, while \(\|D_j\|\) falls faster than any power of \(j\). For small local strength \(J\) the total is at most a quarter of \(\langle\psi,H_0\psi\rangle\). The gap, which is 1 without perturbation, stays at least \(\tfrac34\) minus a negligible amount, and a continuity argument in the coupling closes the loop.
methods.transfer: The result suggests checking for linear, not constant, neighbourhoods in other hierarchical codes, such as welded, layer and fractal constructions, whose stability was doubtful because the usual condition fails. For perturbations with only power-law decay, the polynomial volume factors decide whether the sum converges, so the dilation then matters. The method gives gap stability and ground-space protection and does not by itself control thermal states of the perturbed Hamiltonian.
